opus-5.5.text:
I think Operator is a very interesting signal, but I'd frame it carefully. On the surface it's "an agent that clicks around web pages." What's actually happening underneath is that the model has to look at a screen, a rendered visual interface, and decide what to do next, step by step. That's quite different from the reasoning we saw in o1-style models, which is mostly reasoning in text: math, code, symbolic chains of thought.

The web page is a nice middle ground. It's visual, so you need perception: where is the button, what does this layout mean, is this pop-up blocking me. But it's still a fairly structured, constrained world. The action space is small: click, type, scroll. The feedback is relatively clear: did the order go through or not. So I see it as a training ground. It's not the full physical world, but it forces the model to connect perception, planning and action in a closed loop, which pure language reasoning never had to do.

Why does this matter? Because reasoning in text alone has a ceiling. A lot of real tasks need you to observe the environment, act, see what changed, and adjust. That's essentially the reinforcement learning setting: multi-step decisions, delayed reward, recovering from mistakes. When Operator gets stuck on a weird captcha or a form that behaves unexpectedly, it has to reason about a visual state it has never seen before. That's the beginning of reasoning grounded in the world, not just in tokens.

I'd also be honest about the limitations. Right now these agents are slow, they make silly mistakes, and long-horizon reliability is still poor. If each step is 95% reliable, a 30-step task fails most of the time. So the key technical problem isn't just better vision. It's better RL: training on lots of interactive trajectories so the model learns to explore, check its own progress, and backtrack. In that sense, web and computer use is to agents what math and code were to reasoning models. It's an environment where you can define reward and scale up training.

And looking further out, if you can reason reliably over screens, the natural next step is reasoning over camera input in the physical world, robots and embodied agents. The interface changes, but the core capability is the same: perceive, think, act, get feedback, keep going. So I'd say Operator isn't the destination. It's a first real step from "the model thinks" to "the model does," and the visual web is the first playground where that's happening at scale.

r001.rationale: It describes Operator as a step from text-based reasoning toward reasoning grounded in visual interfaces and the world.

r002.rationale: It describes web pages as visual interfaces with buttons, layouts, and actions, but does not characterize them primarily as a visual presentation of text.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Operator is interesting less for what it does today and more for what it quietly admits. For years the dream was that a model would understand the world through pixels, the way we do. Operator takes a more pragmatic route: the web page is a kind of half-structured visual world. It has layout, buttons, text, images, but underneath it there's a DOM, there's HTML, there's semantics the agent can lean on. So it's a training ground where visual perception doesn't have to carry the whole burden. The model can see a screenshot, but it can also cheat a little by reading the structure.

From a reinforcement learning perspective, that's actually exactly what you want in an early stage. The web gives you a huge, diverse, but relatively clean environment with clear rewards: did you book the ticket, did you fill in the form, did you land on the right page. You don't have to deal with lighting, occlusion, physics, all the mess of the physical world. So I see it as a stepping stone. It lets the model practice the loop of look, decide, act, observe, which is the core of embodied reasoning, in a setting where the signal is dense enough that you can actually learn from it.

What I'd be careful about is overclaiming. Operating a browser is not the same as reasoning in the visual world in the general sense. A lot of the "visual" competence there is really text competence wearing a screenshot as a costume. The real test is whether the policies learned on web pages transfer when the structure is taken away, when you only have raw pixels and the environment doesn't cooperate. My guess is that some of the planning and error recovery transfers, and the perception part largely doesn't yet. But as a first environment where a language model is forced to act over many steps and live with the consequences, it's a good choice, and I think it's a sign that the field is moving from models that talk about the world to models that have to operate inside it.

r001.rationale: The response presents Operator as a stepping stone from models that merely talk about the world to models that act within it, and describes practicing embodied reasoning through visual interaction.

r002.rationale: It characterizes web pages as a partly structured visual environment and says much of their apparent visual competence is text competence presented through a screenshot.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is that a web page becomes an environment to act in, rather than just a source of text. The system has to look at what’s on the screen, decide what action will move it toward a goal, click or type, and then examine what changed. That creates a loop between perception, reasoning, and action.

For example, locating a button is a visual recognition problem. Understanding whether clicking it will advance your task—and checking afterward whether it actually did—is a reasoning problem. If something unexpected happens, you have to revise your plan.

Web pages are a useful starting point because they’re structured environments designed for human interaction. But they’re still much more constrained than the physical world. So I would see Operator as a step toward reasoning through visual interaction, rather than evidence that the broader problem is solved. The important capability is connecting what you see with what you do, and learning from the result.

r001.rationale: The response calls Operator a step toward reasoning through visual interaction, but does not communicate that this signals OpenAI’s ambition to move beyond purely abstract logical reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response describes web pages as structured environments for interaction, but does not characterize them primarily as visual presentations of text.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as an important step because a web page is more than a piece of text. It has a visual layout, buttons, menus, and a state that changes when you interact with it. An agent has to connect what it sees with what it can do: Where should I click? What happened after that click? Am I closer to completing the task?

That creates a loop of observation, reasoning, action, and feedback. Instead of simply producing an answer, the model has to carry out a sequence of actions and recover when something unexpected happens.

But I would distinguish this from understanding the physical world. Websites are designed for people to use, and their interactions are relatively constrained. The physical world involves much more uncertainty. So I see Operator as a useful testing ground: can a model use visual information to act reliably over many steps? That’s a meaningful capability on the path toward more general agents.

r001.rationale: The response calls Operator a step toward general agents and describes acting on visual information, but it does not clearly frame this as extending intelligence beyond purely abstract logical reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes pages as having visual layouts and interactive controls, but does not characterize them as primarily a visual presentation of text.
